# Pure abnormal stresses: exact section induction and its limits

This note records the lower-dimensional information genuinely supplied
by a pure abnormal whole-space-cover stress. It does not exclude a
budget below OC. Two exact examples explain why section barycenters
and generalized section traces alone do not complete an induction.

## 1. The pure section equations

Use the attained normal-span parameterization of
`candidate da91e18223378a53`.
Let the normalized continuous cap normals u_i lie in V and write

  L_i(z,x)=a_i.z+u_i.x-b_i,  |u_i|=1.

Assume a Fritz John stress with objective coefficient zero has been
obtained. Denote the nonnegative active budget multipliers by r_i,
the active whole-space coverage multipliers by eta_z, and the
consistent effective coarea traces by tau_i. Let

  S_i=int d tau_i,  Z_i=int z d tau_i,  X_i=int x d tau_i.

At each multiplied base, a probability measure nu_z on actual saddle
pairs (x,lambda) supplies p_zi=int lambda_i dnu_z and
q_zi=int lambda_i x dnu_z. Contacts lie in V, satisfy all L_k<=0,
and satisfy lambda_i L_i=0 and sum_i lambda_i u_i=0.

The free offset, base-tilt, and normal equations are precisely

  r_i S_i=sum_z eta_z p_zi,
  r_i Z_i=sum_z eta_z z p_zi,
  r_i P_V X_i=sum_z eta_z q_zi.                          (1)

There is no cap-volume source and no hinge term. The sphere
multiplier is zero: take the scalar product of its unsimplified
equation with u_i, and use the first two equations and L_i=0 on
both section and assigned contact points. The same common-rotation
argument as in the normal theorem gives

  sum_i r_i S_i u_i=0,
  sum_i r_i u_i Z_i^T=0,
  sum_i r_i X_i u_i^T=0.                                (2)

Thus the individual FULL section barycenter is a convex combination
of assigned contacts only when V=R^d. In a lower-rank stratum this
assertion is valid after projecting the continuous coordinate to V;
one cannot silently recover each perpendicular first moment from
the summed tensor equation.

Nevertheless every relevant cap normal lies in V, so (1) gives the
exact cross-margin inequalities

  r_i int L_k d tau_i
     =sum_z eta_z int lambda_i L_k(z,x)dnu_z <=0           (3)

for every k, with equality when k=i. If r_i S_i>0, the projected
section barycenter therefore belongs to all the original closed
cap complements. Its integer base is Z_i/S_i, which need not be
an integer. No center-membership assertion follows from (3).

These equations assume a genuine consistent FJ selection. They do
not assert that arbitrary moment data manufacture such a stress, or
that an abnormal stress exists at every endpoint.

## 2. Each geometric cap section is an actual mixed-convex body

### 2.1 Restrict to the positive-volume base hull first

Let P be the finite nonempty set of integer bases with positive
d-dimensional fiber volume. The cover and stress in Section 1 are
required only above P. One MUST first replace the original body by

  C^+=C intersect (conv(P) x R^d).                        (4a)

This retains every original positive fiber exactly. Moreover
conv(P) intersect Z^n=P. Indeed, if an integer z is a convex
combination of indices in P, the same convex combination of their
positive-volume fibers lies in K_z; Brunn--Minkowski makes it
positive-volume. Thus (4a) removes every originally zero-volume
integer fiber and introduces no new integer base. Cap masses,
hinges, all cap-coefficient derivative functions, and their selected
effective trace integrals are unchanged: an original zero-volume
fiber contributes identically zero to every such cap-mass function.
The whole-space constraints and their contacts at P are unchanged
as well.

Put m=dim aff(P), choose z_0 in P, and let E=aff(P)-z_0. The
lattice Gamma=E intersect Z^n has rank m and is saturated: if
k v belongs to Gamma for a nonzero integer k and v in Z^n,
then v belongs to E and hence to Gamma. Its rank is m because
integer differences of points of P span E.

There is a unimodular integer transformation U sending Gamma to
Z^m x {0}. Here is the elementary basis-extension argument. A
nonzero saturated lattice contains a primitive integer vector:
divide any nonzero vector by the gcd of its coordinates and use
saturation. Integer Euclidean row operations send that primitive
vector to e_1. Subtracting the first coordinate times e_1 from
the other lattice vectors splits off Z e_1. The remaining lattice
in the last n-1 coordinates is again saturated, since k(0,v) in
it implies (0,v) in it. Induction gives the claimed transformation;
the rank-zero case is immediate. The Euclidean row operations are
unimodular, so their composition is too.

Apply z -> U(z-z_0), and then drop the n-m identically zero base
coordinates. The resulting body, denoted C^+ again, is a convex
body in R^m x R^d. To verify full relative dimension, choose m+1
affinely independent indices in P and an open continuous ball
inside each of their fibers. The convex hull of these balls at
their respective bases has nonempty interior in aff(P) x R^d.
For example, fix one interior continuous point above each base;
the m independent base differences and d independent within-fiber
directions span that product affine space. Their small simplex
already has dimension m+d.

Every integer fiber of this reduced body has positive d-volume
and corresponds to a point of the original P. The continuous
coordinate is unchanged in the base transformation, so each
fiber's d-volume and every (d-1)-dimensional continuous section
measure are unchanged. Their finite Hausdorff-measure sums are
unchanged as well, although distances between distinct bases
need not be preserved. Affine cap coefficients transform by
substitution; the constant part is absorbed in b_i. The mass
equation and base-moment equation in (1) transform into the same
equations in the reduced m base coordinates. The continuous
normal span, actual contact coordinates, and all scalar margins
remain unchanged. We henceforth use these reduced coordinates
and again call the transformed base set P.

Explicitly the transformed section base moment is the retained
part of U(Z_i-z_0 S_i); subtracting z_0 times the first equation
of (1) from its second and applying U gives precisely its required
contact balance. This also covers m=0, when there is no remaining
base-moment equation.

This reduction is necessary. For example, the full-dimensional
body conv(({0} x [-1,1]^2) union
({1} x ([-1,1] x {0}))) has positive area only at base zero.
Its section x_2=0 nevertheless has length two at EACH of the
integer bases zero and one. The second section fiber is not a
derivative source for the original area measure and need not be
covered by constraints imposed only at P={0}. Restriction (4a)
removes it before any induction is invoked.

### 2.2 The section after the base reduction

Fix a cap with 0<c_i<M. Its plane crosses the interior of the
reduced C^+: the positive and negative source masses give points
strictly on both sides, which can be replaced by nearby interior
points preserving their strict signs. The segment between those
interior points crosses the plane in int C^+.

Rotate only continuous coordinates so u_i=e_d, and write x=(xi,t).
The section plane is

  t=b_i-a_i.z.

The allowed fiber shear t'=t+a_i.z-b_i fixes the integer coordinates,
preserves the mixed lattice, and has determinant one. Dropping its
identically zero coordinate on the section identifies C^+ intersect
{L_i=0} with a convex body C_i in R^m x R^(d-1). Its integer fiber
sections are isometric to their xi coordinates. In particular their
(d-1)-dimensional Hausdorff measure is exactly ordinary fiber volume.
Every nonempty integer section fiber has base in the transformed P,
so the original whole-space coverage constraints apply to it.

For a nonunit original normal the identical construction uses its
unit direction; the coarea trace is 1/|u_i| times this mixed section
volume. This is one CONSTANT for the entire section, so normalized
depth and all section fractions are unaffected. The construction
does not use ambient (m+d-1)-dimensional volume.

The restriction of any other cap is exactly

  (a_k-u_(k,d) a_i).z+u_(k,perp).xi
                         >=b_k-u_(k,d)b_i.               (4)

It is either a genuine closed ambient halfspace in the reduced
space, the whole space, or the empty set. Vertical reduced caps
and caps containing an entire section are retained.

## 3. A legitimate consequence of OC in continuous dimension d-1

Suppose the effective trace tau_i is the FULL geometric coarea
section measure of the RETAINED reduced body C^+ and S_i>0.
This holds, for example, when every nonempty section at a retained
integer fiber is a proper cut, with no
supporting-facet coincidences. Then its intrinsic dimension is
exactly d-1 and tau_i is, up to the common coarea constant, the
measure required by OC for the actual reduced body C_i.

An elementary cover observation is important. The caps OTHER than
i cover the ENTIRE affine hyperplane L_i(z,x)=0 at every z in P.
If a point there had L_k<0 for all k!=i, moving it a sufficiently
small distance in direction -u_i would make every margin negative,
contradicting the assumed whole-space cover at that base. This
argument uses the finite number of caps and handles closed
boundaries without replacing them by open caps.

Assume OC has been proved in continuous dimension d-1 for all
integer dimensions, in particular for (m,d-1), and put

  kappa=gamma_(d-1)/2^m >=gamma_(d-1)/2^n,   gamma_0=1.

It supplies a SINGLE point y_i of the actual mixed section whose
depth for tau_i is at least kappa. Some other cap k contains y_i
by the preceding cover observation: its base necessarily belongs
to P by Section 2.1. Formula (4) and OC then give

  tau_i(H_k) >= kappa S_i  for some k!=i.                 (5)

If the reduced ambient dimension is zero, the section is a single
point and this assertion follows directly with kappa=1. Whole and
empty restricted caps cause no exception.

Thus the normalized cross-section matrix

  B_ik=tau_i(H_k)/S_i

has B_ii=1 and, on every row meeting the full-trace hypotheses,
max_(k!=i) B_ik>=kappa. At the same time (3) controls the FIRST
MOMENTS of these same restricted margins. This is the exact new
lower-dimensional constraint. Neither (3) nor (5) identifies y_i
with the section barycenter, nor gives an ambient cap-volume bound.

## 4. At facet coincidences the effective trace need not satisfy OC

The full-trace hypothesis is necessary. Here is an exact continuous
counterexample even with the effective trace's centroid in the
actual section. Let T be a planar triangle with centroid zero,
vertices p_1,p_2,p_3, and barycentric coordinates lambda_i. Put

  C=T x [0,1] subset R^3,  H={t>=0},  epsilon=1/10,
  T_i={x in T:lambda_i(x)>=1-epsilon},
  theta(x)=(1/3)sum_(i=1)^3 1_(T_i)(x).                  (6)

This theta is a genuine effective section density in the Clarke
gradient of the cap mass at H. To see it, perturb its margin to

  t+delta[(1-epsilon)-lambda_i(x)],  delta>0.

Its proper cutting sections converge to the bottom facet exactly
over T_i; the physical cap-gradient moments converge to those of
1_(T_i) dx. Coarea factors tend to one. Averaging these three
limiting gradients is permitted in the convex Clarke gradient
set and gives precisely theta. Continuous-normal normalization,
if imposed, changes neither the limiting trace nor its moments.

The three T_i are disjoint homothetic copies of T with area
epsilon^2|T|. Therefore the trace tau=theta dx has mass
epsilon^2|T| and centroid zero. Each homogeneous canonical cap

  G_i={lambda_i>=1/3}

contains exactly T_i from the trace support and misses the other
two pieces. These three caps cover the full plane because the
affine barycentric coordinates sum to one. Consequently every
point has tau-depth at most 1/3.

The origin has depth at least 1/3. Indeed, for any nonzero linear
functional ell let m=max_i ell(p_i)>0. Since sum p_i=0, every
ell(p_j)>=-2m. If p_i realizes m, the whole cluster
T_i=(1-epsilon)p_i+epsilon T has ell at least
(1-3epsilon)m>0. Every through-origin cap therefore contains an
entire cluster, of one third of the trace mass. Hence

  max_y depth_tau(y)=1/3 < gamma_2=4/9.                   (7)

The geometric section is the convex triangle T and has ordinary
uniform measure; its effective trace is the nonuniform subdensity
(6). Its centroid, support-plane equation, and legitimate cap
gradient status do not turn it into the uniform source required
by the induction hypothesis. This example has cap fraction one
and is not asserted to be a below-target FJ minimizer. It disproves
the proposed inference from section-trace or barycenter data alone.

## 5. A pure abnormal endpoint can have no section mass at all

There is also an exact example at an ACTUAL whole-space hinge
minimum where an admissible pure abnormal stress has S_i=0 for
every multiplied cap. Use n=2,d=1, P={0,1}^2 and

  K_z=[epsilon_z L-1/2,epsilon_z L+1/2],  L>1/2,
  epsilon_00=epsilon_11=1,
  epsilon_10=epsilon_01=-1.

These are the exact fibers of their convex hull, since the four
binary bases are extreme points of the projection. Their total
mass is M=4. With N=2, the caps x>=0 and x<=0 form a whole-line
cover, each has mass two, and both geometric sections are empty.

For completeness their hinge is the global minimum 4L. Any
two-cap whole-line cover has thresholds x>=a(z), x<=b(z), where
a,b are affine and a<=b on P. Its hinge is at least

  4L+sum_(epsilon=-1)b(z)-sum_(epsilon=1)a(z) >=4L,

because b>=a and every affine function on the binary square has
equal sums on its two diagonals. The displayed zero thresholds
attain the bound. No two-cap cover has budget less than 1/2 by
the union bound, so tau=1/2 is the actual endpoint of feasibility.

Both cap-mass functions are locally constant at these parameters:
the plane is separated from all four compact fibers. Thus their
physical gradients are zero. Choose objective multiplier zero,
one active cap-budget multiplier r_+=1, r_-=0, all eta_z=0, and
zero sphere multipliers. This is a nonzero normalized FJ stress
and satisfies all equations (1)--(3), but supplies no positive
lower-dimensional source to which induction could apply.

There is also an objective-one stress at this example; pure
abnormality is not forced. The budget 1/2 is far above its OC
target 1/8, and its continuous rank is one. Thus the example
does not refute a stronger argument using the below-target and
minimality hypotheses to SELECT a useful nonzero section stress.
It does rule out treating an arbitrary abnormal endpoint stress
as automatically furnishing such a source.

## 6. What remains to close an induction

For full geometric traces AFTER restricting to the positive-base
hull and reducing its saturated lattice rank, (5) is a rigorous use
of lower-dimensional OC, with exact coarea and all oblique
restrictions tracked. To turn
it into an ambient cap-budget contradiction would require an
additional link between these section overlaps, their margin first
moments, and the ORIGINAL d-dimensional cap masses. No such link
is proved here. At nonsmooth facets one must additionally control
or replace the selected subdensities, and pure abnormality alone
does not even ensure that their total weighted mass is positive.
